sources: 2 Kings 25:8-11 (the Babylonians burned the house of the Lord and Jerusalem, broke down its walls, and carried the people into exile, 587/586 BC)
Lamentations 1:1 (“How the city sits solitary, that was full of people!”)
Lamentations 3:21 (“This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope”)

Lamentations 3:22-23 (“It is because of the Lord’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness”), lightly modernized
Lamentations 3 sits at the center of the book’s five chapters; it is an acrostic of 66 verses
Tradition links Lamentations to Jeremiah (the Greek Septuagint’s heading; Talmud, Bava Batra 15a)
In Jewish tradition, Lamentations (Eikhah) is read on Tisha B’Av, the fast mourning the temple’s destruction
In Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran tradition, Lamentations is chanted at Tenebrae, the night prayers of the last three days of Holy Week
Thomas O. Chisholm, “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” (1923), music by William M. Runyan, based on Lamentations 3:22-23
Shot 5’s “the Lord’s loving kindness never runs out” follows the common modern rendering of 3:22 (e.g. ESV “The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases”)
check: Painting NM2 shows the poet face-hidden because tradition names Jeremiah, a prophet; confirm that is the right caution.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever had a season where everything seemed to fall apart?
options: i’m so sorry. sit with me. this one was written in a season like yours.
then you know. listen to what this poet found.
i’m glad. keep this one for someone who is.

steps.line: Jerusalem had fallen. The Babylonian army burned the temple and the city, and many of its people were taken far away.
steps.label: 2 Kings 25:9-11

steps.line: A poet sat in the ruins and wrote songs of grief. Jewish and Christian tradition links them to the prophet Jeremiah. The book is called Lamentations.
It begins, “How lonely the city sits, that was once full of people!” Most of the book is grief, and it doesn’t hide it.
steps.label: Lamentations 1:1

steps.q: Four of the book’s five poems are alphabet poems: each verse starts with the next Hebrew letter. Why write grief that way?
o: To grieve it all, from A to Z
steps.why: Many readers hear it as grief told completely, from the first letter to the last, and a shape held steady when everything else fell apart.

steps.q: Then, near the very middle of the book, the poet turns. What do you guess he says?
steps.why: Lamentations 3:21, in the book’s central and longest poem: a triple alphabet, three verses for every Hebrew letter.

steps.line: Then, near the very middle of the book, the poet turns: “This I call to mind, and so I have hope.”
steps.label: Lamentations 3:21

steps.q: The poet says God’s mercies are “new every morning.” Why every morning, and not once and for all?
o: Each day’s trouble gets fresh mercy
Yesterday’s mercy ran out by night
Mercy has to be earned again each day
steps.why: Not because yesterday’s ran out: the same verse says it never does. Some readers hear manna in it, fresh each morning, enough for today.

steps.line: “The Lord’s loving kindness never runs out. His mercies don’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.”
steps.label: Lamentations 3:22-23

steps.q: When Jews read Lamentations aloud each year, they don’t end on its last, sad verse. What do they do?
o: Repeat the hopeful verse before it
Skip ahead to a psalm of thanks
steps.why: On Tisha B’Av the verse before the end is said again: “Turn us back to You, Lord, and we shall return; renew our days as of old.”

say: here’s what i love. this hope wasn’t written after things got better. it was written in the ruins.
in jewish tradition it’s read each year on the day of mourning for the temple, and many churches read it in the days before easter. its promise: God’s mercy starts over every morning.

steps.q: The poet still sits in the same ruins. Nothing around him has changed. So where does his hope come from?
o: He sees signs the city will rise again
He chooses to stop feeling sad
He remembers who God has always been
steps.why: “This I call to mind.” His hope isn’t in what he sees. It’s in what he remembers about God.

today.say: tomorrow morning, before you check your phone, name one mercy that’s new today, even a small one. if you’d like, make it a one-line morning prayer, “great is your faithfulness,” or listen to the old hymn of that name: watch, learn, or join in. your choice.
options: good. the morning will be new. it always is.
then this one’s yours. one small mercy, every morning.
